README.md.content:
# Report service

Design-only workspace. Read docs/product.md and docs/deployment.md, then inspect
the current API and database contract. No dependencies or external access are needed.
Current service functions use injected database access and throw errors for the
HTTP adapter to map. Production implementation and deployment are outside this task.

docs/deployment.md.content:
# Deployment constraints

Database migrations deploy before application code. Old and new application versions
overlap during rollout, and the application can be rolled back independently of the
database. Mobile clients continue to use GET /reports/:id for signed-in reads.
The HTTP adapter currently applies authentication to every registered route.

docs/product.md.content:
# Report links

A signed-in user may create a link to a report owned by their tenant. Anyone with
the link can read that report without signing in. The link expires after 24 hours;
the tenant may revoke it sooner. Links must continue to work across service restarts
until expired or revoked. Existing signed-in report access must keep working.
This release does not include report editing, share analytics, or link delivery by email.

DESIGN.md.content:
# Revocable report sharing

This document proposes the implementation; it does not authorize implementation or deployment. The source contracts are `docs/product.md`, `docs/deployment.md`, `src/reports.js`, `src/routes.js`, and `db/schema.sql`.

## Outcome and boundaries

A signed-in tenant member can create a bearer link for a report belonging to that tenant. Possession permits anonymous reading of that report for exactly 24 hours from creation, unless the tenant revokes the link first. Share records survive application restarts. Keep `GET /reports/:id`, its authentication requirement, tenant check, and `{ id, body }` response unchanged for mobile clients.

Use a persisted opaque token rather than a self-contained signed token: revocation already requires authoritative persisted state, so a signed token would add key rotation and verification complexity without removing the lookup. Process-local tokens cannot meet restart persistence. Editing, analytics, and email delivery are outside this release.

Routine choices: each creation makes a distinct link; revocation targets one link; any authenticated member of the owning tenant may create or revoke it, matching the brief's tenant-level authority. Shared reads return the current report body using the existing projection. No snapshot or new role hierarchy is introduced.

## API and adapter contract

| Endpoint | Authentication | Successful result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /reports/:id` | Required, unchanged | 200 existing report projection |
| `POST /reports/:id/shares` | Required | 201 `{ shareId, url, expiresAt }` |
| `DELETE /reports/:id/shares/:shareId` | Required | 204, including repeated authorized revocation |
| `GET /shared-reports/:token` | Explicitly public | 200 `{ id, body }` |

The create response supplies the non-secret management identifier and the bearer URL once; the caller retains `shareId` to revoke. No link list or token recovery endpoint is required. A lost creation response may be retried to create another independent link; it does not extend an earlier link's lifetime. This release does not promise idempotent creation.

`src/routes.js` owns route registration. Add explicit authentication metadata, for example `authentication: 'public'`, on the single anonymous GET route. The HTTP adapter must enforce authentication by default for missing metadata and apply a public exception only to that registered method and route. It must not exempt all report routes or use a broad path-prefix bypass. The adapter's implementation is absent from this fixture; locating and changing it is a required implementation dependency, not an optional follow-up. Existing parameter extraction must be extended to pass `reportId`, `shareId`, or `token` under the service argument names; an anonymous request must not need a fabricated `user`.

Use the existing injected-database service style. Keep `readReport` intact and add cohesive share functions in `src/reports.js` (or a feature-local sharing module if its size warrants separation). Services throw errors; the adapter maps explicit new error codes to HTTP responses while preserving the existing `Not found` mapping. Missing authentication on protected routes maps to 401. Missing reports, cross-tenant resources, and unknown share identifiers map to 404. Unknown, malformed, expired, revoked, or orphaned public tokens share the same generic 404 response. Database failures map to a generic 503 and must never authorize a read.

Creation URLs use a deployment-configured public HTTPS origin, never an untrusted request Host header. Shared responses, including errors, use `Cache-Control: no-store` and `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`. Disable response caching for these endpoints at intermediaries; redact bearer tokens in access/error logs and tracing. The token grants access, so it must not appear in analytics or exception payloads. A later revocation cannot retract a body already downloaded or copied.

## Persistent state and service operations

Add a `report_shares` table through an additive migration. Proposed logical fields are `id` (text primary key), `report_id` (foreign key to reports), `token_hash` (unique, non-null), `created_at`, `expires_at`, and nullable `revoked_at`. Use the database's supported UTC timestamp representation consistently, with an expiry constraint equivalent to `expires_at > created_at`. The injected adapter maps these fields to camelCase as it does for reports. Choose a foreign key with cascade deletion so a deleted report leaves no usable shares; public reads also require the report to exist. Database engine and migration tooling are not present, so exact DDL and timestamp functions must be confirmed at implementation time.

Generate 32 random bytes per bearer token using the runtime's cryptographic random source, encode as canonical base64url, and store only its SHA-256 digest. Use a separate random share identifier. Return the raw token only inside the creation URL after the insert commits. Retry a uniqueness conflict with newly generated values; cap retries and fail rather than reuse a colliding token. All SQL arguments are bound parameters.

Creation performs tenant-scoped report lookup and insertion in one transaction, with a report lock or equivalent protection against concurrent ownership change/deletion. Set `created_at` using database time and `expires_at = created_at + 24 hours`; callers cannot select expiry or tenant identity. A failed or ambiguous commit must not produce a confirmed successful link response. No in-memory map or process secret is required for later validation.

Anonymous reading hashes a bounded, canonical token and executes a single authoritative query joining the share and report where `revoked_at IS NULL` and database time is strictly before `expires_at`. Return only the existing report projection. Do not split validation and report retrieval across cached or replica-stale reads. Equality with expiry is expired. The required adapter operation is conceptually `findActiveSharedReport(tokenHash)`; token validity and the report body are resolved together.

Revocation first verifies the requested report belongs to `user.tenantId`, then updates only the share whose identifier and report identifier match. Use a transaction or equivalent tenant-scoped atomic operation. Set `revoked_at` once and retain it on retries; already revoked or expired shares still return 204 to the owning tenant. An unknown share returns 404. Tenant B cannot revoke Tenant A's link even with its management identifier. Commit before returning success.

The database is the authority for time and revocation. After a successful revoke response, subsequent validity queries must reject the token; route them to a consistency source that observes that commit, not an asynchronously replicated reader. A read whose validity query precedes revocation may finish afterwards. This is the concurrency boundary; revocation does not cancel in-flight responses. Report tenant identity is treated as stable under the current contract. If ownership transfer is later introduced, it must revoke shares atomically before exposing the report to its new tenant.

Expired/revoked rows may remain without affecting correctness. Cleanup is optional and must not become an availability dependency. Restarts require no rebuilding of active links and must preserve the configured public origin and database connection.

## Deployment, compatibility, and rollback

1. Deploy the additive table and indexes first. Do not alter `reports` or existing response shapes. Old code ignores the new table, and a database rollback is unnecessary when application code rolls back.
2. Deploy the adapter authentication change and share-capable application together, with link creation disabled until public reads and tenant revocation are reachable. Verify anonymous versus authenticated routing before enabling creation.
3. During old/new overlap, route all three new endpoint patterns only to share-capable instances. Existing signed-in report reads may continue across both versions. If the deployment platform cannot provide this routing, keep creation disabled until all serving instances support sharing. Blindly load-balancing active share URLs to old instances is not a valid rollout.
4. Enable creation only after the routing, database, origin, and authentication checks pass. Verify a link created by one instance works through another and after restarting its creator.
5. An application rollback retains the additive schema and all share records. To preserve issued links, retain compatible public-read and revoke handlers (for example the last share-capable pool with endpoint routing) until every issued link has expired or been revoked. Disable new creation first. A complete rollback to the original code alone cannot serve existing anonymous links because it has no public route; do not claim uninterrupted sharing in that configuration. Deployment owners must provide the compatible serving path as a release gate. Emergency removal of sharing would be a deliberate availability tradeoff requiring a separate decision.

No destructive migration, framework replacement, or new external service is needed. The HTTP adapter and deployment routing owners must participate because repository service changes alone cannot satisfy the brief.

## Acceptance evidence for implementation

- Existing mobile GET responses and same-tenant/cross-tenant authentication behavior remain unchanged. Missing route metadata remains protected; only the exact public GET allows anonymous access.
- Tenant A can create and revoke its report links; Tenant B cannot create/revoke them or use guessed report/share identifiers to reveal report data. A bearer link intentionally works without a session.
- A valid link returns the report; malformed/unknown/revoked tokens and missing reports receive indistinguishable 404 responses. No token is persisted in raw form or exposed by logs.
- With controlled database time, reads just before 24 hours succeed, reads exactly at or after expiry fail. Client clocks do not affect validity. Repeated reads do not extend expiry.
- Repeated authorized revocation succeeds, mismatched report/share identifiers fail, and two independent links can be revoked independently. A read started after acknowledged revocation fails; document the permitted in-flight race.
- Database integration tests exercise committed creation, uniqueness conflicts, rollback on insert failure, concurrent deletion, and failed database reads. Persistence tests create a link, restart the service, and read it from another instance using the same database.
- Adapter tests exercise parameter mapping, protected POST/DELETE, the anonymous GET, error mapping, no-store headers, origin construction, and token redaction. Test the real adapter, not only direct service calls.
- Deployment validation runs old code against the migrated schema, mixed-version endpoint routing, creation gating, and application rollback with the retained compatible handlers. Confirm no intermediary serves cached content after revocation.

This fixture has no executable tests, HTTP adapter implementation, migration runner, or rollout configuration. The above are delivery gates, not completed test claims. This design was checked against the five source contracts; implementation, migration execution, and deployed-runtime behavior remain unverified.
